interactions.label: Why are anaerobic bacteria unable to survive in oxygenated environments?

params.question: Why are anaerobic bacteria unable to survive in oxygenated environments?

answers.text: They produce excessive reactive oxygen species that damage their own DNA

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Anaerobes do not produce excessive ROS themselves; rather, they are unable to neutralise the reactive oxygen species generated in oxygenated environments because they lack the necessary protective enzymes.

answers.text: They lack catalase and superoxide dismutase, enzymes that neutralise oxidative damage

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! Anaerobes lack catalase and superoxide dismutase — two enzymes that protect cells from reactive oxygen species. Without these defences, exposure to oxygen causes lethal oxidative damage, which is why anaerobes thrive only in low-oxygen environments such as dead tissue and abscesses.

answers.text: Their cell walls contain lipids that are oxidised and destroyed by molecular oxygen

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The fundamental reason is the absence of catalase and superoxide dismutase, not cell wall lipid oxidation. Without these enzymes, anaerobes have no mechanism to detoxify reactive oxygen species.

answers.text: They require carbon dioxide instead of oxygen for their electron transport chain

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Some bacteria are capnophilic (CO₂-requiring), but anaerobic bacteria specifically cannot tolerate oxygen because they lack catalase and superoxide dismutase to neutralise oxidative damage — a distinct mechanism.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key concept is that anaerobes lack catalase and superoxide dismutase — enzymes that neutralise reactive oxygen species. Without these, oxygen exposure causes lethal oxidative damage, explaining why they survive only in low-redox environments such as dead tissue, abscesses, and poorly perfused wounds.

Excellent! The absence of catalase and superoxide dismutase is the key reason anaerobes cannot tolerate oxygen — they have no defence against reactive oxygen species, which is why they thrive in devitalised, ischaemic tissue.

interactions.label: Which feature best distinguishes erysipelas from cellulitis?

params.question: Which feature best distinguishes erysipelas from cellulitis?

answers.text: Erysipelas has sharply demarcated, raised borders; cellulitis has diffuse, poorly defined margins

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! Erysipelas involves the upper dermis and superficial lymphatics, producing a sharply demarcated, raised, bright red plaque. Cellulitis extends deeper into the lower dermis and subcutaneous tissue, causing diffuse, poorly defined redness — as the infection goes deeper, the borders become less distinct.

answers.text: Erysipelas involves the subcutaneous tissue; cellulitis is confined to the upper dermis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect — this is reversed. Erysipelas involves the upper dermis and superficial lymphatics, while cellulitis extends deeper into the lower dermis and subcutaneous tissue.

answers.text: Erysipelas is caused by Staphylococcus aureus; cellulitis is caused by Group A Streptococcus

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect — the organisms are reversed. Erysipelas is caused by Group A Streptococcus (S. pyogenes) and is treated with penicillin. Cellulitis typically involves Staphylococcus aureus and is treated with nafcillin or cloxacillin.

answers.text: Erysipelas produces gas in the tissues; cellulitis does not

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Neither erysipelas nor cellulitis produces gas in the tissues. Gas formation in soft tissues is a hallmark of clostridial infections such as gas gangrene caused by Clostridium perfringens.

overallFeedback.feedback: Erysipelas and cellulitis differ primarily in depth: erysipelas involves the upper dermis with sharply demarcated, raised borders, while cellulitis extends into the subcutaneous tissue with diffuse, poorly defined margins. Remember the pattern — as infection goes deeper, borders become less distinct and treatment more aggressive.

Well done! The sharp versus diffuse border distinction reflects the depth of infection — superficial erysipelas has well-defined raised edges, while deeper cellulitis has blurred margins. This depth principle organises the entire SSTI classification.

params.question: Why does haematogenous osteomyelitis in children preferentially involve the metaphysis of long bones?

answers.text: The metaphysis has rapid bone turnover that provides abundant nutrients for bacterial growth

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. While rapid bone turnover does occur at the metaphysis during growth, the reason for bacterial seeding is the sluggish blood flow and absence of phagocytic immune cells in the metaphyseal vascular loops — not nutrient availability.

answers.text: The metaphysis has sluggish blood flow and lacks phagocytic cells, creating a bacterial sanctuary

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! The metaphyseal vessels form hairpin loops where blood flow slows dramatically, and this region lacks resident phagocytic cells. Together, these create a sanctuary where blood-borne bacteria can settle and multiply without being cleared by the immune system.

answers.text: The metaphysis has the thinnest cortical bone, allowing bacteria to penetrate easily from the periosteum

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. In haematogenous osteomyelitis, bacteria arrive via the bloodstream, not through the cortical bone surface. Thin cortex is relevant to contiguous spread or subperiosteal abscess extension, not haematogenous seeding.

answers.text: The metaphysis is the only region of long bones that receives a haematogenous blood supply

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. All regions of long bones receive blood supply. The metaphysis is special because its vascular loops create areas of sluggish flow where bacteria can settle without effective immune clearance.

overallFeedback.feedback: In children, the metaphyseal blood vessels form hairpin loops with sluggish flow, and the region lacks phagocytic immune cells. This combination creates a 'bacterial sanctuary' where blood-borne organisms can seed and grow without being cleared — explaining the predilection of childhood osteomyelitis for this site.

Exactly right! The metaphyseal vascular loops create an immune-privileged zone — sluggish flow lets bacteria settle, and absent phagocytes let them multiply unchecked. This is why the metaphysis of the femur, tibia, and humerus are the commonest sites.

interactions.label: While performing a slit-skin smear for leprosy diagnosis, why must the examiner

params.question: While performing a slit-skin smear for leprosy diagnosis, why must the examiner pinch the skin firmly before making the incision?

answers.text: To concentrate the bacilli in the dermis by compressing the surrounding tissue

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Pinching does not concentrate bacilli. The purpose is to squeeze blood out of the tissue — blood in the sample would dilute and obscure the acid-fast bacilli, making them difficult to identify on Ziehl-Neelsen staining.

answers.text: To anaesthetise the area through sustained pressure, reducing patient discomfort

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Pinching does not provide anaesthesia. The purpose is to make the site bloodless so that the dermal tissue fluid collected contains bacilli-laden macrophages without being diluted by blood.

answers.text: To squeeze blood out of the area, preventing it from diluting and obscuring the bacilli

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! Firmly pinching the skin creates a bloodless field. Blood in the sample would dilute the dermal tissue fluid and obscure the acid-fast bacilli on Ziehl-Neelsen staining. The SSS collects dermal tissue fluid — where bacilli reside within macrophages — not blood.

answers.text: To make the epidermis taut so that the blade can make a clean, uniform slit

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. While taut skin is easier to incise, the specific reason for the pinch in SSS is to expel blood from the area. A blood-contaminated sample would dilute and obscure the bacilli on staining.

overallFeedback.feedback: The pinch technique expels blood from the sampling site. Blood would dilute the dermal tissue fluid and obscure the acid-fast bacilli on Ziehl-Neelsen staining. The SSS collects tissue fluid from the dermis, where M. leprae bacilli reside within macrophages — a bloodless field is therefore critical for diagnostic accuracy.

Well done! Creating a bloodless field is essential — the SSS aims to collect dermal tissue fluid containing bacilli-laden macrophages, not blood. This is why the technique scrapes the slit walls for tissue fluid after the blood has been squeezed out.
